Problem 1: Chain on a sphere

A uniform chain of length $L$ is fixed by one end at the top of a smooth spherical surface of radius $R$, with $L < \pi R/2$ (Fig. 11). The upper end of the chain is released.

2. At which point of the chain will the tension force $T$ be maximal immediately after release?

Problem 2: Motion without slipping

A long board of mass $m_1$ rests on the smooth horizontal surface of a table; a block of mass $m_2$ is placed on the right end of the board. The block is connected to the wall by a light unstretched spring of stiffness $k$. A load of mass $M$ is attached to the board by means of a light inextensible thread passed over a pulley (Fig. 12). At the initial moment the system is at rest. There is dry friction between the board and the block. The coefficient of friction between the board and the block is $\mu$.

Problem 3: Heat engine

For a heat engine operating on the Carnot cycle, the temperature of the heater is $T_1 = 800\,\mathrm{K}$, and the temperature $T$ of the cooler depends on the useful power $P$ of the engine. The cooler is a massive body, thermally insulated from the surroundings, which by means of heat conduction transfers to a cold reservoir at temperature $T_2 = 300\,\mathrm{K}$ all the heat energy $Q_2$ received during the time $\Delta t$ of operation of the engine (Fig. 13). The heat conduction obeys the law $Q_2 = \alpha(T - T_2)\Delta t$, where $\alpha = 1.0\,\mathrm{kW/K}$.

1. Express the power $P$ of the heat engine in terms of the temperatures $T_1$, $T$ and $T_2$.

2. Calculate the temperature $T_m$ of the cooler at which the power of the engine is maximal.

3. Determine this maximal power $P_{\max}$.

4. Find the efficiency $\eta$ of the heat engine when it operates at maximal power.

problems.title: Problem 5: Unipolar inductor
problems.problem:
Problem 5: Unipolar inductor

A unipolar inductor is a rapidly rotating permanent magnet in the form of a disc. The disc is made of a magnetic alloy capable of producing a strong magnetic field, and it is coated with a thin conducting layer of nickel.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/russia-2010-1-5-fig1.png

Fig. 15

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/russia-2010-1-5-fig2.png

Fig. 16

When the disc rotates, a potential difference arises between the rotation axis and the lateral surface, which can be measured with a stationary voltmeter (Fig. 15). If, on the other hand, a battery is connected to the rotation axis and the lateral surface, the magnet will start to rotate rapidly, having turned into an electric motor. In just the same way, if the shaft of an ordinary electric motor is rotated rapidly, it turns into a generator, and conversely, if a voltage is applied to an electric generator, it turns into an electric motor.

Figure 16 shows the scheme of such a really working unipolar electric motor, whose rotor is a strong permanent magnet in the form of a disc of radius $r_0 = 2\,\mathrm{cm}$ mounted on an axle. When a battery with EMF $\mathscr{E} = 1.5\,\mathrm{V}$ is connected by means of sliding contacts, the disc starts to rotate rapidly.

1. What will the stationary voltmeter in Fig. 15 show at a rotation frequency of the disc $\nu = 3000\,\mathrm{rev/min}$? What is the polarity of this potential difference? Indicate the polarity in Fig. 15.

2. Neglecting friction, estimate the limiting rotation frequency (in rev/min) of the magnetized disc (the rotor of the unipolar motor in Fig. 16). Indicate the direction of rotation of the rotor for the polarity of the battery and the direction of the vector $\vec{B}$ given in Fig. 16. The magnitude of the vector $\vec{B}$ is constant and equal to $B = 1\,\mathrm{T}$.

Note. To simplify the calculations, assume that in the conducting nickel layer the magnetic induction vector $\vec{B}$ is perpendicular to the surface of the disc (Fig. 15). Also, to simplify, assume that the current in the conducting layer flows along the radius.

3. Let $\mu = \mu_{\min}/2$. In this case the load $m_1$ and the board $m_2$ will move with different accelerations. After what time $t$ from the start of the motion will the load slide off the board?

Assume that $m_1 = M = 1\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m_2 = 2\,\mathrm{kg}$. Take the length of the board $L$ equal to $1\,\mathrm{m}$. It is known that the length of the load is much smaller than $L$. Take the free-fall acceleration equal to $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

problems.title: Problem 2: Dissociation

Problem 2: Dissociation

Under normal conditions oxygen consists of diatomic molecules $\mathrm{O_2}$. When the temperature is raised, some of the molecules may dissociate, as a result of which two $\mathrm{O}$ atoms are formed from each $\mathrm{O_2}$ molecule. Figure 6 shows two identical cyclic processes 1 and 2 in the coordinates $(\rho, p)$, where $\rho$ is the density of the gas and $p$ is the pressure. The dimensionless quantities $p/p_0$ and $\rho/\rho_0$ are plotted on the axes, where $p_0$ and $\rho_0$ are some scale factors. In the first experiment the working substance was molecular oxygen $\mathrm{O_2}$ (low temperatures). The second experiment was carried out at considerably higher temperatures. In it, part of the oxygen was in the molecular ($\mathrm{O_2}$) state and part in the atomic ($\mathrm{O}$) state, and the degree of dissociation did not change during the experiment. The mass of the gas was the same in both experiments. It is known that the ratio of the maximal temperatures in these experiments is $k_{\max} = T_{2,\max}/T_{1,\max} = 5.0$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/russia-2010-2-2-fig1.png

Fig. 6

1. Determine the degree of dissociation $\alpha$ (the fraction of dissociated molecules) of the oxygen molecules in the second experiment.

2. Determine the ratio $k_{\min}$ of the minimal temperatures in these experiments.

problems.title: Problem 4: Electric hotplate

Problem 4: Electric hotplate

An electric hotplate has two coils (two heating elements), which can be connected to the mains either separately, or by connecting them in series or in parallel. We shall assume that the resistances of the coils do not depend on temperature.

It turned out that if only the first coil is connected to the mains, the hotplate heats up to the temperature $t_1 = 180\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and if only the second coil is connected, the hotplate heats up to the temperature $t_2 = 220\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

To what temperature will the hotplate heat up when:

1. the coils are connected in series,

2. the coils are connected in parallel.

Hint. The heat flow from the hotplate to the surroundings is proportional to the temperature difference between the hotplate and the air in the room. The air temperature is to be considered constant and equal to $t_0 = 20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

A thin-walled cylinder of length $L = 1.50$ m, closed at the bottom, is installed vertically. At its upper part it is connected to another cylinder of much larger diameter (Fig. 13). In the lower cylinder, at a distance $h_1 = 380$ mm from the upper edge, there is a thin light piston. Because of the large difference between the diameters of the cylinders, the change $\Delta h$ may be neglected for displacements of the piston along the whole length of the lower cylinder.

It follows from the statement of the problem that the piston is in equilibrium. Is this equilibrium position stable? Are there other equilibrium positions? If there are, at what distances $h_i$ from the piston to the upper edge? Are these equilibrium positions stable? One may assume that for small changes of the volume under the piston the temperature of the helium remains constant.

Problem 2: Nanomelting

The melting temperature of a bulk sample of tin is $t_0=232\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The melting temperature of very small tin spheres of diameter $d=20$ nm turns out to be 25 degrees lower and equal to $t_d=207\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. This is the so-called size effect; moreover, it has been established experimentally that the melting temperature depends not only on the size but also on the shape of the sample. At what temperature will a tin foil of thickness $h=d$ melt?

Assume that the tin atoms in the surface layer, of thickness 2–3 interatomic distances, possess some excess energy compared with the energy of the atoms in the bulk, and that the heat of fusion $\lambda$ per atom is proportional to the mean binding energy $U$ of the atoms in the substance and to the absolute temperature $T$ of the phase transition (melting): $\lambda \sim U \sim T$.

Unfortunately, the position of the origin of coordinates has been lost. Explanatory notes indicated that $C_d=1.000$ J/K, $C_a=0.715$ J/K, and also that
$$T_c-T_b=2(T_b-T_a)=200\ \mathrm{K}, \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{p_c}{p_a}=\frac{V_c}{V_a}.$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/russia-2014-1-3-fig1.png

1. Find the work $A$ done by the gas per cycle and the efficiency $\eta$ of the cycle.

2. Determine the values of the temperatures $T_a$, $T_b$ and $T_c$.

3. Draw the graph of the cycle in the coordinates $(p,V)$ and determine the amount of substance $\nu$.

Note. A process with constant heat capacity $C$ is called polytropic, and for it the relation
$$pV^n=\mathrm{const}$$
holds, where $n$ is a constant, the polytropic index.

On hot summer days, when the temperature in the room had settled at $t_0 = 30^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the experimenter Glück noticed that the operating time of the refrigerator motor had become twice the idle time. Having decided to optimize its operation, the experimenter used the regulator to change the temperature inside the refrigerator by $\Delta\theta = 9~^\circ\mathrm{C}$. As a result, the idle time became twice the operating time. Determine:

1. To what temperatures $t_1$ and $t_2$ was the regulator set at the beginning and at the end of the experiment?

2. To what internal temperature $t_m$ must the regulator be set for the refrigerator motor to start working without interruption?

3. At what temperature $t_3$ set by the regulator will the switching-on frequency of the refrigerator become maximal?

Hint: The regulator sets the temperature $t$ inside the refrigerator within a small interval $t \pm \Delta t/2$. When the temperature inside becomes equal to $t + \Delta t/2$, the refrigerator motor switches on; when it falls to $t - \Delta t/2$, it switches off. Assume that:

1) the power of the heat supplied is proportional to the difference between the temperature inside the refrigerator and that of the surroundings and is constant over the whole interval of internal temperatures $t \pm \Delta t/2$.

2) the thermal power removed by the motor from the internal volume of the refrigerator during its operation does not depend on the temperatures.

3) the change of the temperature in the room can be neglected.

Problem 5: Solar sail

A solar sail is a flat mirror of mass $m=1.660\,\mathrm{g}$ and area $S=1.000\,\mathrm{m^2}$. The sail is oriented perpendicular to the sun's rays and moves along the line passing through the centre of the Sun and the centre of the mirror. At the initial moment of time it is at a distance $R_0=1\,\mathrm{a.u.}$ from the Sun. At what distance $R_1$ from the Sun will the sail be after $t_1=1$ hour of flight, if it moved with a constant but unknown velocity $v\ll c$?

The solar constant $W_0=1.367\,\mathrm{kW/m^2}$ is the total flux of solar radiation passing per unit time through a unit area oriented perpendicular to the flux at a distance of $1\,\mathrm{a.u.}$ from the Sun.

Note. Did you know that the length of a year equals $\pi\cdot 10^7\,\mathrm{s}$ to within half a percent?

Problem 3: Water and ice

As is well known, at atmospheric pressure water begins to freeze, and ice to melt, at the temperature $t_0=0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. At pressures higher than atmospheric, water can be in the liquid phase at lower temperatures as well. An increase of the pressure by $133\,\mathrm{atm}$ lowers the melting temperature of ice by $1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. In the initial state, water of mass $m_0=1\,\mathrm{kg}$ and a very small amount of ice are in equilibrium in an adiabatic shell under the pressure $p_1=200\,\mathrm{atm}$. In an adiabatic process the pressure is slowly decreased to atmospheric pressure $p_0=1\,\mathrm{atm}$.

1. Find the change $\Delta m_{\mathrm{i}}$ of the mass of ice.

2. Find the change of the volume of the water + ice system.

3. What work does the system do against the external pressure when it is decreased from $p_1$ to $p_0$?

The specific heat capacity of water is $c_{\mathrm{w}}=4.2\,\mathrm{J/g}$, that of ice $c_{\mathrm{i}}=2.1\,\mathrm{J/g}$. The specific heat of fusion of ice is $q=336\,\mathrm{J/g}$. The densities of water and ice at atmospheric pressure are $\rho_{\mathrm{w}}=1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, $\rho_{\mathrm{i}}=0.9\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

The compressibility of water is $G=-\frac{1}{V}\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta P}=5\cdot 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$; the compressibility of ice is smaller than the compressibility of water.

problems.title: Problem 1: The slower you go...

Problem 1: The slower you go...

In calm weather a series of tests of a radio-controlled model of a boat with a petrol engine was carried out on a lake; during the tests it was found that at a speed $v_1=5.00\,\mathrm{km/h}$ the fuel consumption per unit distance is $\lambda_1=20.0\,\mathrm{g/km}$, and at a speed $v_2=15.0\,\mathrm{km/h}$ the consumption is $\lambda_2=40.0\,\mathrm{g/km}$. • What is the maximum time $\tau_x$ for which the engine of a stationary model can run?
• At what speed $v_0$ of the model is the fuel consumption per unit distance minimal, and what is its value $\lambda_0$? The results obtained must be found with an error not exceeding 1%.
• What is the maximum distance $L_0$ the model can travel, and in what time $\tau_0$?
• What values $\tau_1$ can the time taken by the model to cover the distance $L_1=3\,\mathrm{km}$ take?

Problem 2: Substances X and Y

Then, having ensured reliable thermal insulation of the vessel, the external pressure is increased slightly. Let us denote this state by «B».

problems.title: Problem 1: Where will the ball fall?

Problem 1: Where will the ball fall?

From a boat moving downstream along a river, a metal ball is lowered into the water. The ball falls onto the river bed at a horizontal distance $l_1$ from the place where it was lowered into the water. If the ball is lowered into the water from a boat moving upstream, the ball falls onto the bed at a distance $l_2$ downstream. For a boat crossing the river along a trajectory perpendicular to the current of the river, the distance to the point where the ball falls onto the bed is $l_3$.

1. What is the distance to the point where the ball falls onto the bottom for a boat moving on a lake of the same depth as the river?

2. How many times is the speed of the boat greater than the speed of the current?

In a reactor, in an aqueous solution of some substance, heat is released as a result of a chemical reaction with power $N=5\,\mathrm{kW}$. To regulate the temperature in the reactor, air is blown through tubes with small holes laid on the bottom of the reactor. The pressure of the air supplied to the reactor can be taken equal to atmospheric pressure $P_0=10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$, and its temperature equal to the room temperature $T_0=22\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Determine the volumetric flow rate of air $q$ needed to maintain in the reactor a temperature $T<T_K$, where $T_K=100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is the boiling temperature of the aqueous solution at atmospheric pressure. Assume $T_K-T\ll T_K$. Determine the numerical value of $q$ for $T=95\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

The molar heat of vaporization of water at temperature $T$ is known: $\lambda=40\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. The saturated vapour pressure of water near $T_K$ changes practically linearly with the coefficient $\alpha=3.5\,\mathrm{kPa}/^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The saturated vapour pressure above the solution corresponds exactly to the saturated vapour pressure of water. The heat going into heating the air can be neglected. The pressure drop across the tube carrying the gas out of the reactor is negligibly small. In the absence of air supply to the reactor there is no heat exchange with the surroundings.

Problem 1: Crawling strip

Using a special technology for treating polymer materials, one can achieve anisotropy of the properties of their surface. For example, the motion of a polyethylene strip on a horizontal table surface in the direction $AB$ (in Fig. 1, to the right) is characterised by the friction coefficient $\mu_1$, and the motion in the direction $BA$ by the friction coefficient $\mu_2<\mu_1$. If a strip of length $l$ lying on the table is subjected to cyclic heating and cooling, one can notice that the strip moves over the surface of the table.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/russia-2021-2-1-fig1.png

[In the figure, Fтр denotes the friction force.]

Fig. 1

1. In which direction ($AB$ or $BA$) will the strip move after a large number of cycles?

2. Over what distance will the strip move in $N$ heating–cooling cycles if the difference between the maximum and minimum temperatures in a cycle is $\Delta T$? Write the answer as a formula.

3. Calculate the distance over which a strip of length $l=20\,\mathrm{cm}$ moves in $N=100$ heating–cooling cycles if its temperature changes by $\Delta T=80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The values of the friction coefficients are $\mu_1=0.15$, $\mu_2=0.05$.

Assume that when the temperature of the polyethylene changes by $\Delta T$, its length changes by the amount $\Delta l=\alpha l\Delta T$, where $l$ is the length of the strip at room temperature and $\alpha=2\cdot10^{-4}\,^\circ\mathrm{C}^{-1}$ is the coefficient of thermal expansion of polyethylene. Problem 3: What does an ohmmeter measure?
problems.problem:
Problem 3: What does an ohmmeter measure?

According to one of the models of an ohmmeter, it consists of an ideal source of constant voltage $\mathscr{E}$ (with zero internal resistance) and, connected in series with it, a resistor of resistance $r$ and an ideal ammeter (Fig. 2). When the resistor under investigation is connected to terminals $A$ and $B$, the built-in ammeter shows a current which is then converted into the value of the measured resistance and displayed on the indicator of the ohmmeter. If a diode whose current–voltage characteristic is shown in Fig. 3 is connected to the terminals of such an ohmmeter, it will show the resistance $R_D=6\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/russia-2021-2-3-fig1.png

Fig. 2

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/russia-2021-2-3-fig2.png

Fig. 3

If a resistor of resistance $R=20\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ is added in series to this diode and the resistance of the resulting pair is measured with the ohmmeter, it will show $R_1=30\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$. If instead of the resistor and the diode an ideal battery of voltage $U_B=3\,\mathrm{V}$ is connected to the ohmmeter (the polarity of the connection is unknown!), it will show a negative resistance $R_B=-7.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ ($R_B<0$). From these data determine:

1. the value of the voltage $\mathscr{E}$ of the internal source of the ohmmeter;

2. the value of the internal resistance $r$ of the ohmmeter;

3. the voltage $U_0$ at which the diode opens;

4. the reading $R_{B1}$ of the ohmmeter when the same battery is connected to it, but with the polarity reversed.

Note: the ammeter built into the ohmmeter measures the current taking its direction into account. If the current flows through the ammeter in the reverse direction, its value is taken as negative. The ohmmeter performs all calculations taking signs into account.

problems.title: Problem 1: Three tigers

Problem 1: Three tigers

At the initial moment of time the tigers form a right triangle with legs equal to $L$ (Fig. 1). Assume that the sizes of the tigers are much smaller than $L$. The magnitude of the velocity of the first tiger is $v_1=v$, where $v$ is a known quantity, and the speeds of the second and third tigers $v_2$ and $v_3$ are such that during the motion the angles in the triangle $ABC$ formed by the tigers remain constant.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/russia-2023-1-4-fig1.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/russia-2023-2-5-fig1.png

The rod is rigidly connected to the centre of puck 2 and cannot rotate relative to it. The rod is connected to puck 1 by a tight fit on a smooth hinge, the radius of whose axle is much smaller than the radius of the rod, so that puck 1 can rotate freely relative to the rod.

The rod makes an angle $\alpha=30^\circ$ with the normal to the wall. The rod is rigid and weightless. The length of the rod is $L=0.8\,\mathrm{m}$. The radii of the pucks are much smaller than the length of the rod. The radius of the rod is much smaller than the radii of the pucks. The pucks are identical and homogeneous.

The construction is given a velocity $v_0=2.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ directed along the rod towards the wall, and after some time puck 2 collides with the wall.

1. Show that during the impact the forces acting on the pucks from the rod can be considered to be directed along the rod.

Use this fact in answering the subsequent questions, even if you have not been able to justify it.

2. Determine the angular velocity of rotation of the rod immediately after a perfectly elastic collision of puck 2 with the wall (the wall is smooth).

3. Determine the angular velocity of rotation of the rod immediately after a perfectly inelastic collision of puck 2 with the wall. The coefficient of friction between the puck and the wall is $\mu$. Consider two values of the coefficient of friction: $\mu_1=0.2$ and $\mu_2=0.6$.

Note: In a perfectly inelastic collision the component of the velocity of puck 2 perpendicular to the wall becomes zero.

problems.title: Problem 1: Lift-off
problems.problem:
Problem 1: Lift-off

A small ball of mass $m$ was placed on a smooth horizontal surface. A light inextensible thread was attached to it, passed over a light pulley of negligibly small radius, and a load of mass $M$ was suspended from its other end (see figure). The system was released from rest (the state shown in the figure by the dashed line). At some moment of time, when the thread is inclined to the horizontal at an angle $\alpha$, the ball leaves the surface, and the acceleration of the load at this moment of time is zero. There is no friction in the axle of the pulley.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/russia-2023-3-1-fig1.png

1. Find the ratio $m/M$.

2. Find $\sin\beta$ of the angle of the thread to the horizontal at the initial moment of time.

problems.title: Problem 2: Aquarium on springs
problems.problem:
Problem 2: Aquarium on springs

A side wall of a cubic thin-walled aquarium $(a\times a\times a)$ broke. It was decided to press a new wall $(a\times a)$ in place with spring clamps. The first spring, of stiffness $2k$, was fixed at the middle of the upper edge of the new wall, and the second spring, of stiffness $k$, at the middle of the lower edge. After that the aquarium was moved up to a vertical wall (see figure).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/russia-2023-3-2-fig1.png

All surfaces at the places of contact of the new wall with the aquarium are flat and smooth. The new wall is rigid, completely covers the adjoining side walls and the bottom, and is parallel to the plane of the wall. The friction force at the place of contact of the wall with the table is negligibly small. The lengths of the springs in the undeformed state are the same.

1. What must the minimum compression of the springs be so that the aquarium can be filled to the brim with water of density $\rho$?

During the filling, consider the aquarium to be at rest, and water does not leak at the places of contact of the wall with the aquarium.

2. What will the minimum compression of the springs become if they are interchanged?

Consider the acceleration due to gravity $g$ to be known.

problems.title: Problem 3: Refrigerator
problems.problem:
Problem 3: Refrigerator

In a thin-walled cylindrical vessel of inner radius $R$, under a piston, there is a column of water of height $h_1$ at temperature $t_0=0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The piston and the bottom of the cylinder are thermally insulated. The power of heat losses through the side walls is proportional to the area of contact and to the difference between the temperatures of the contents of the vessel and of the surroundings, $N=\alpha\cdot S\Delta t$, where $\alpha$ is a known constant. The cylinder is placed vertically in a refrigerator whose initial temperature is $t_1<0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Then the temperature in the refrigerator is changed in such a way that the piston of the cylinder moves with a constant speed. The ice forming in the cylinder does not hinder the free motion of the piston. Moreover, the ice does not float up above the surface of the water but rests against the piston, being completely immersed in the water, from time to time breaking away from the walls of the vessel. The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is $\lambda$, the density of water is $\rho_w$, the density of ice is $\rho_i$.

1. Determine in which direction and with what speed $v$ the piston moves.

2. Find for what time interval $\tau_{\max}$ such motion continues.

3. Establish the dependence of the temperature $t$ in the refrigerator on time $\tau$ in the time interval $[0,\,\tau_{\max}]$. Express it in terms of $h_1$, $t_0$, $t_1$, $v$, $\tau$.

4. Find the temperature at the moment of time $\tau_{\max}$. Express it in terms of $t_0$, $t_1$, $\rho_w$, $\rho_i$.

problems.title: Problem 4: Direct current
problems.problem:
Problem 4: Direct current

In a simplified model, a direct-current source consists of an ideal source of constant voltage $U_0$ and a resistor of resistance $r$ connected in series (see Fig. 1). When the direct-current source is connected into a circuit containing resistors of resistance $R\ll r$, the current can be considered to be $I_0\approx U_0/r$.

The electric circuit is a wire mesh consisting of links of equal resistance $R$. Three links have been replaced by identical direct-current sources $I_0$ (see Fig. 2).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/russia-2023-3-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1 [Рис. 1 = Fig. 1]
